# Pharyngeal cancer

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Head and neck surgery > Pharyngeal cancer*

[Original Article Link](/library/Cj0qcT)

---

## Summary

Pharyngeal cancers include <u>malignant tumors</u>, most commonly <u>squamous cell carcinomas</u>, of the <u>nasopharynx</u>, <u>oropharynx</u>, <u>hypopharynx</u>, or <u>tonsils</u>. <u>Alcohol</u> and tobacco use are the two most important <u>risk factors</u> for pharyngeal cancer. Other <u>risk factors</u> include certain viral infections (e.g., <u>HPV</u> in the <u>oropharynx</u>), poor oral hygiene, and workplace-related exposures (e.g., radiation). Clinical presentation varies based on the location of the <u>tumor</u>. Symptoms may include a growing cervical lump, persistent <u>sore throat</u>, <u>dysphagia</u>, and/or a change in voice. Diagnosis is confirmed with tissue <u>biopsy</u>, and staging is determined via imaging modalities such as CT or <u>MRI</u>. Treatment usually requires <u>surgery</u>, <u>radiation therapy</u>, and/or <u>chemotherapy</u>. Posttreatment monitoring is indicated for all patients with <u>advanced cancer</u> because of high recurrence rates.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Oropharyngeal cancer</u> [[1]](/library/WKcP2W0)

* <u>Incidence</u>: an estimated 54,010 new cases in the US in 2021

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (2:1)

* <u>Nasopharyngeal cancer</u> [[2]](/library/cKca2W0)

* <u>Nasopharyngeal cancer</u> is rare in the United States (< 1:100,000)

* Most common in patients of Mediterranean and southern Chinese (including Hong Kong) descent

* About 85% of all new cases are diagnosed in Asia. [[3]](/library/eKcx2W0)

* <u>Hypopharyngeal cancer</u>: uncommon condition [[4]](/library/1Kc22W0)

* <u>Incidence</u>: 2,500 new cases in the US annually

* Peak age: between 50–60 years of age




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* <u>HPV infection</u>

* <u>Tobacco product</u> use (including smokeless products)

* <u>Alcohol</u> use

* <u>Nitrosamine</u> consumption from salted/preserved foods

* <u>Obesity</u>

* Chronic <u>iron deficiency</u>

* Long-term consumption of <u>carcinogenic</u> food (e.g., <u>aflatoxin</u>)

* Exposure to radiation

* Associations

* <u>Nasopharyngeal carcinoma</u>: <u>EBV infection</u>

* <u>Oropharyngeal carcinoma</u> and <u>tonsillar cancer</u>: <u>human papillomavirus infection</u>

* Diseases causing <u>atrophy</u> of the <u>mucosa</u> (e.g., <u>Plummer-Vinson syndrome</u>)





> [!TIP]
> The combined use of <u>alcohol</u> and <u>tobacco products</u> compounds the risk of either. [[5]](/library/E2d8j60)

---

## Clinical features

Pharyngeal cancer is usually asymptomatic for a long time . Often, the first manifestations are swollen cervical <u>lymph nodes</u>.




![Sections of the pharynx](media/jfurb56fgp1ybv1m9afbnbhc.jpg)

Sections of the pharynx




### Oropharyngeal cancer and hypopharyngeal cancer




* Common early symptom: local <u>lymph node</u> <u>metastases</u> causing enlarged cervical <u>lymph nodes</u>

* Foreign body sensation, <u>dysphagia</u>, <u>sore throat</u>

* Muffled voice

* Severe <u>ear</u> <u>pain</u>





![Hypopharyngeal cancer](media/dou0h7ulbb3gb77v1varjl3f.jpg)

Hypopharyngeal cancer




### Nasopharyngeal cancer [[2]](/library/cKca2W0)




* Painless <u>lymphadenopathy</u>

* Unilateral nasal discharge, <u>nosebleeds</u>, impaired nasal breathing (due to obstruction)

* Obstruction of the <u>Eustachian tube</u>: recurrent <u>otitis media</u> (may be accompanied by effusion); <u>conductive hearing loss</u>, <u>tinnitus</u>

* Infiltration of <u>caudal</u> <u>cranial nerves</u> → <u>Garcin syndrome</u>

* <u>Sore throat</u>

* <u>Headache</u>





### Tonsillar cancer




* Persistent <u>sore throat</u>, <u>globus sensation</u>, <u>dysphagia</u>

* Unilateral <u>otalgia</u>

* Unilaterally indurated, ulcerated, and/or enlarged tonsil

* Enlarged cervical <u>lymph nodes</u>

* <u>Halitosis</u>

* Blood-tinged <u>sputum</u>

* <u>Trismus</u> (sign of local invasion)





### <u>Metastatic</u> disease



* See “<u>Clinical features of oral cavity cancer</u>” for details.




References: [[6]](/library/TF06h3)

## Diagnosis

### Initial workup [[5]](/library/E2d8j60)




* Clinical evaluation

* Rule out features consistent with <u>deep neck infection</u>, e.g., rapid onset, <u>features of tonsillopharyngitis</u>.

* Initiate a prompt referral to otolaryngology for patients with suspected pharyngeal cancer.

* Endoscopy with <u>biopsy</u> (typically <u>FNA</u>): for direct visualization of the <u>pharynx</u> and <u>larynx</u>

* Histopathologic evaluation

* Confirms the diagnosis and the type, grade, and extent of the <u>tumor</u>

* <u>Pleomorphic</u> cells and <u>mitotic figures</u> demonstrate a <u>neoplastic</u> change from <u>dysplasia</u> to <u>SCC</u>. [[7]](/library/VHcG6d0)





### Further workup [[5]](/library/E2d8j60)




* <u>HPV testing</u>

* <u>FNA</u> samples from the <u>oropharynx</u> are tested for <u>high-risk HPV</u> <u>mRNA</u>.

* Overexpression of p16 suggests an <u>HPV</u>-associated <u>malignancy</u>.  [[5]](/library/E2d8j60)[[8]](/library/w2dhP60)

* Imaging

* Staging imaging if <u>malignancy</u> is confirmed

* <u>MRI</u> and/or CT of the neck with IV contrast: to assess <u>tumor</u> anatomy

* <u>FDG-PET/CT scan</u>: to assess for distant <u>metastasis</u>





![Hypopharyngeal cancer](media/ottyclss5ua3x5nshtl6xhf4.jpg)

Hypopharyngeal cancer

## Treatment

### General principles [[5]](/library/E2d8j60)[[9]](/library/D2d1P60)




* Individualize treatment in consultation with a multidisciplinary <u>tumor board</u>.

* Treatment is based on patient factors such as <u>TNM stage</u>, comorbidities, <u>performance status</u>, and <u>goals of care</u>.

* Options include <u>radiation therapy</u>, <u>chemotherapy</u>, and/or surgical resection and reconstruction.

* Following treatment, monitor for recurrence at regular intervals.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Surgery</u> or <u>radiation therapy</u> alone can be curative in patients with small nonmetastatic tumors.




> [!WARNING]
> A patient with pharyngeal <u>carcinoma</u> is at risk for <u>airway obstruction</u>. See “<u>Airway management in head and neck cancer</u>” before <u>procedural sedation</u> and/or <u>airway</u> manipulation.




### Locoregional disease [[1]](/library/WKcP2W0)[[2]](/library/cKca2W0)[[4]](/library/1Kc22W0)




* <u>Oropharyngeal cancer</u> [[1]](/library/WKcP2W0)

* <u>Radiation therapy</u> or <u>surgery</u>  for small tumors without nodal involvement

* <u>Surgery</u> and <u>adjuvant radiotherapy</u>, with or without concurrent <u>chemotherapy</u> for locally advanced disease  [[1]](/library/WKcP2W0)

* <u>Nasopharyngeal cancer</u> [[2]](/library/cKca2W0)

* High-dose <u>radiation therapy</u> with <u>chemotherapy</u>

* <u>Surgery</u> (<u>neck dissection</u>) for persistent or recurrent <u>lymph nodes</u> in patients with controlled primary <u>tumor</u>

* <u>Hypopharyngeal cancer</u> [[4]](/library/1Kc22W0)

* Surgical resection (laryngopharyngectomy and <u>neck dissection</u>) with <u>adjuvant radiation therapy</u>

* Additional <u>chemotherapy</u> for locally advanced disease





> [!TIP]
> Treatment aims to apply the most effective curative method while ensuring the best possible preservation of function, i.e., voice preservation, <u>airway mechanics</u>, and <u>swallowing</u>. [[7]](/library/VHcG6d0)




### <u>Metastatic</u> or recurrent disease [[7]](/library/VHcG6d0)[[9]](/library/D2d1P60)




* Resectable localized disease: surgical resection ± adjuvant therapy (<u>chemotherapy</u> and/or <u>radiation therapy</u>)

* Unresectable localized disease: <u>radiation therapy</u> or <u>chemoradiotherapy</u>

* <u>Metastatic</u> disease

* Curative intent: <u>platinum-based chemotherapy</u>, and/or <u>cetuximab</u> or <u>cancer immunotherapy</u> (e.g., <u>nivolumab</u>, <u>pembrolizumab</u>)  [[7]](/library/VHcG6d0)

* Palliative intent: <u>palliative chemotherapy</u> and/or <u>radiation therapy</u>





### Posttreatment monitoring [[10]](/library/v2dAj60)




* All patients should undergo regular history, physical, and endoscopy to assess for recurrence.

* Order posttreatment imaging for selected patients.

* T3/T4 or N2/N3 disease: baseline imaging of the primary site with <u>FDG-PET/CT scan</u> within 6 months of treatment [[10]](/library/v2dAj60)[[11]](/library/x2dEP60)

* Any stage with signs of recurrent disease: repeat imaging

* Assess <u>thyroid</u> function (e.g., <u>TSH</u> levels) every 6–12 months after <u>radiation therapy</u>. [[10]](/library/v2dAj60)





> [!TIP]
> For patients who received <u>radiation therapy</u>, measure <u>TSH</u> every 6–12 months to assess for <u>thyroid</u> complications. [[10]](/library/v2dAj60)
